script.opening: “The worms are back. Third time. The chemist keeps giving me tablets for the kids and they just come back. I need tablets for all of us this time — me too, I’m itching as well.”

facts.text: Nadia with Leila, 6, on the bed beside her in a small room. Sami, 18 months, is asleep in a travel cot behind them.

Itchy bottom at night for a week, waking her up. Nadia saw tiny white moving threads on the toilet paper and on her bottom with a torch. Leila is sore from scratching, a bit red between the cheeks and at the front. No bleeding, no discharge, no pain on passing urine, eating well, no tummy pain, no weight loss.

Twice in four months the pharmacy sold a single chewable tablet for Leila (and once for Sami, who was refused because he was under 2). Nobody else was treated. No one explained hygiene or a second dose.

Nine weeks in emergency temporary accommodation after leaving a privately rented flat with mould. One room for the three of them; shared bathroom and toilet on the corridor with other residents; no washing machine; the launderette costs £5 a load. The council said it was “for a couple of weeks”.

facts.topic: Nadia’s own health (only if asked about pregnancy or breastfeeding)
facts.text: 22 weeks pregnant, seeing the midwife. Not breastfeeding. Itching around her own bottom for a few days.

facts.topic: The worry (only if asked gently what else is on her mind)
facts.text: “The men on the corridor use the same toilet. Leila is scared to go at night on her own. She’s sore at the front too. Could it be… could someone have done something to her?” Leila has said nothing worrying; she is never left alone in the shared bathroom; no change in behaviour except fear of the corridor at night.

Tired and anxious, apologetic about the room. Relieved if the doctor explains why worms keep coming back without blame. Becomes quiet when the safeguarding worry comes up; grateful if it is taken seriously but not catastrophised. Very keen on any letter that might help with housing.

ice.ideas: “The tablets don’t work properly, or we keep catching them from the other people here.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: that Leila’s soreness means she has been abused by someone on the corridor; also shame about the room, and worry about taking tablets in pregnancy.
ice.expectations: “Tablets for all of us, including me and the baby. And I want to know she’s safe.”

cues: “Third time” — recurrence: reinfection because the household was not treated together and hygiene measures were not explained.
“Me too” — ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding before offering medicines.
A small room with a travel cot and a shared bathroom — temporary accommodation and what is realistic.
Hesitation about “anything else” — the safeguarding worry.

checkpoints.text: Confirms the typical features (nocturnal perianal itch, worms seen) and asks about red flags and vulval symptoms; explains that threadworm can cause vulval itching in girls
Asks about pregnancy and breastfeeding and the ages of all household members before recommending treatment

Recommends treating all household members at the same time: mebendazole for those aged 2 and over (single dose, repeat after 2 weeks if infection persists; check the SPC/local formulary), considers off-label use for Sami at 18 months, and advises hygiene measures alone for 6 weeks for the pregnant mother

Gives practical hygiene advice for 6 weeks adapted to a shared bathroom and no washing machine (nails short, handwashing and nail scrubbing, morning bath or wash of the perianal area, close-fitting underwear at night, separate towels, damp-dusting)
Explores the safeguarding worry calmly: who has access, any disclosure, behaviour change, bleeding or discharge; explains that threadworm can explain the soreness but that the worry is valid

Makes a proportionate safeguarding plan: no current indicators of abuse, safety planning for night-time toilet use, clear routes if anything is disclosed, discussion with the practice safeguarding lead and health visitor

Acts on the housing: offers a letter supporting a move (families with children should not be in shared-facility B&B-type accommodation for more than 6 weeks), and informs the midwife and health visitor with consent
Avoids blame, involves Leila appropriately, checks understanding and safety-nets (persistent symptoms, abdominal pain, weight loss, vaginal discharge or bleeding, any disclosure)

worked.txt: “The tablet kills the worms but not the eggs, and the eggs get onto fingers and back into mouths. So if only one person is treated and there’s no hand-washing routine, the eggs just go round again. It isn’t about the room being dirty.”
“Before I suggest any tablets for you: is there any chance you’re pregnant, or breastfeeding?”

“Leila gets a tablet now, and a second one in two weeks if she’s still itchy. Sami is under 2, so I’ll prescribe it for him, which is off-licence but commonly done. For you, because you’re pregnant, the advice is no tablet: the hand-washing routine for six weeks does the job.”

“Short nails, scrub under them, hands washed after the toilet and before food. A quick wash of her bottom each morning in the room with a bowl is fine. Tight pants at night. Your own towels, not the shared ones.”

“You were right to tell me. Worms often make girls sore at the front as well, so this fits. Has she said anything, or changed in any way? If she ever does, you call me or 999. I’d also like our safeguarding lead and the health visitor to know you’re in shared accommodation.”

“A family with children shouldn’t be in a room with a shared bathroom for more than six weeks. I’ll write a letter you can give the council saying why this matters for your health and the children’s.”

f.learning: Recurrent threadworm is usually reinfection, not treatment failure. Mebendazole kills the worms but not the eggs, which survive on hands, nails, bedding and surfaces for up to two weeks, so the whole household should be treated at the same time and everyone should follow hygiene measures for 6 weeks. CKS: offer mebendazole to household members aged 2 and over as a single dose, repeated after 2 weeks if infection persists (check the SPC/local formulary); children aged 6 months to 2 years can be treated off-label; pregnant women (especially in the first trimester), breastfeeding women and children under 6 months should use hygiene measures alone for 6 weeks. Always ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding before advising treatment for adults. Threadworm commonly causes vulval itching and soreness in girls, but a parent’s worry about sexual abuse must be explored calmly and taken seriously: ask about disclosure, behaviour change, bleeding, discharge and who has access, and know when to discuss with the safeguarding lead or refer. Families in temporary accommodation with shared facilities face real barriers to hygiene advice, so adapt it to what is possible. In England, B&B-type accommodation with shared facilities should not be used for families with children for more than 6 weeks (Homelessness (Suitability of Accommodation) Order 2003), so a supporting letter and involvement of the health visitor and midwife are part of good care. UKHSA guidance sets no exclusion from school for threadworm.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Hello Leila. What’s brought you both to see me today?
model.why: Greets mother and child; open question

model.text: The worms are back. Third time. The chemist keeps giving me tablets for the kids and they just come back. I need tablets for all of us this time, me too, I’m itching as well.
Third time is really frustrating. Let’s work out why it keeps happening, and then sort out the right thing for each of you. Tell me what you’ve noticed with Leila this time.
Itchy bum at night, she wakes up scratching. I saw the little white threads with a torch. She’s red and sore, at the front too.
Any bleeding, any discharge from the front, pain when she wees, tummy pain or weight loss?
No, none of that. She’s eating fine.
Worms quite often make girls sore at the front as well, because they wander. What happened with the treatment before?
Just one tablet for Leila each time. They wouldn’t give one for Sami, he’s too little. Nobody else.

That’s the key. The tablet kills the worms but not the eggs, and the eggs get onto fingers and go round the family again. It’s nothing to do with being dirty. Who else lives with you, and how old are they?
Just me, Leila and Sami, he’s 18 months. In this one room.
And for you, before I suggest anything: is there any chance you’re pregnant, or are you breastfeeding?
I’m 22 weeks pregnant.
Congratulations. That changes what I’d advise for you, so I’m glad I asked. Tell me about where you’re living at the moment.
It’s a hostel. Temporary. Nine weeks now. We share the bathroom and toilet down the corridor. No washing machine.
That’s hard with two little ones and a baby on the way. Is there anything else worrying you about Leila? You seemed to hesitate.
(quietly) The men on the corridor use the same toilet. She’s scared to go at night. And she’s sore at the front. Could someone have done something to her?
Thank you for telling me, that took courage, and it’s a sensible thing to ask. Has Leila said anything to you, or seemed different in herself? Is she ever in the bathroom on her own?
No, she hasn’t said anything. I always go with her. She’s just scared of the corridor.
Leila, is there anything that’s worried you or made you sad here? You can always tell Mummy or a teacher.
(Leila) The corridor is dark.

What you’ve told me fits worms, and I can’t see anything that makes me think someone has hurt her. But your instinct matters. Keep going with her at night, and if she ever says anything, call me or 999. I’d like to let our safeguarding lead and your health visitor know about your living situation so you have support. Is that okay?
Yes. Okay.

For treatment: Leila has a tablet now and another in two weeks if she’s still itchy. Sami is under 2, so I’ll prescribe his; it’s used off-licence at his age but it’s commonly done. For you, because you’re pregnant, the advice is no tablet. The hygiene routine for six weeks clears it, because the worms only live about six weeks.
No tablet for me? But I’m itching.

I know. The routine really does work, and it protects the baby from an unnecessary medicine. Short nails, scrub under them, wash hands after the toilet and before eating. Wash everyone’s bottoms each morning, a bowl in the room is fine. Snug pants at night. Your own towels.

And the room: families with children shouldn’t be in shared-bathroom accommodation for more than six weeks. I’ll write a letter for the council explaining the health side. I’ll also let your midwife know.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Tablets for Leila and Sami now, again in two weeks if needed. No tablet for me, just the washing and nails for six weeks. You’ll write to the council and tell the health visitor.
Exactly. If anyone’s still itchy after the six weeks, if Leila gets tummy pain, weight loss, a discharge or bleeding, or if she ever says something that worries you, contact me straight away.

social.t: Shared bathrooms, no laundry and overcrowding make hygiene measures hard and increase stress. Ask about housing in any recurrent infection.
Families in hostels often feel judged. Saying clearly that worms are not about dirt helps engagement.

legal.t: In England, B&B-type accommodation with shared facilities should not be used for families with children for more than 6 weeks (Homelessness (Suitability of Accommodation) Order 2003). A GP letter can describe the health impact.
Treating a child aged 6 months to 2 years with mebendazole is off-label. Explain this to the parent and record it (GMC prescribing guidance).

professional.t: Take a parent’s worry seriously, ask the right questions, document, and discuss with the safeguarding lead. Do not dismiss or catastrophise.
Informing the midwife and health visitor, with consent, connects support for the pregnancy and the toddler.

community.t: Health visitors support families in temporary accommodation and can help with practical needs and advocacy.
Pharmacists sell mebendazole for people aged 2 and over; they should ask about pregnancy and age, and refer under-2s and pregnant women.

redFlags: Vaginal bleeding or discharge, or a disclosure: consider abuse or other causes; safeguarding discussion or referral
Abdominal pain or weight loss: reconsider the diagnosis
Persistent symptoms after household treatment and 6 weeks of hygiene measures: review
psychosocial: Child’s fear of the corridor at night
ice: Idea: tablets don’t work or they catch it from others
Concern: abuse; being judged; medicines in pregnancy

playbook.diagnosis: “This is threadworm again, from reinfection because only one person was treated each time. Worms explain the soreness at the front too. Nothing you’ve told me suggests someone has hurt her, but we’ll keep that door open.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The worms lay tiny eggs around the bottom at night. They get on fingers and go back into mouths, so they go round the family. The tablet kills the worms, the washing routine stops the eggs.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted tablets for everyone and to know Leila is safe. Here’s what is right for each of you, and here’s how we’ll keep an eye on her safety.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the worry; plan night-time toilet safety; housing letter; health visitor and midwife involvement.
sharedPlan: Mebendazole for Leila now; repeat in 2 weeks if infection persists (check the SPC/local formulary)
Mebendazole for Sami (18 months) off-label, explained and recorded
Mother (22 weeks pregnant): hygiene measures alone for 6 weeks
Hygiene for everyone for 6 weeks, adapted to the shared bathroom
Safeguarding lead discussion; health visitor informed with consent
safetyNet: Abdominal pain, weight loss, vaginal discharge or bleeding
Any disclosure or new worry: contact the practice, or 999 if a child is in immediate danger

pitfalls.intro: Treating worms is simple. The marks are in getting pregnancy and age right, making hygiene advice realistic, and responding well to a mother’s fear about abuse.

items.fail: Not asking about pregnancy or breastfeeding.
items.why: Pregnant women should use hygiene measures alone.
items.fix: Ask before advising any adult treatment.

items.why: Reinfection from untreated household members is why it recurs.
items.fix: Treat everyone at the same time, by age.

items.why: It cannot be followed in one room with a shared bathroom.
items.fix: Adapt it to the family’s facilities.

items.why: Abuse can be missed and trust is lost.
items.fix: Ask about disclosure, behaviour, access, bleeding and discharge; discuss with the safeguarding lead.

items.why: It drives both the recurrence and the family’s wellbeing.
items.fix: Offer a letter and involve the health visitor and midwife.

items.why: The child’s voice is part of safeguarding.
items.fix: Ask her gently, in words she understands.

timeMap.d: Third time. Agenda: everyone in the family.
Symptoms and red flags; previous treatment; household ages; pregnancy and breastfeeding; housing.
Follow the hesitation. Abuse concern: disclosure, behaviour, access, bleeding, discharge. Speak to Leila.
Treat by age and pregnancy; realistic hygiene; proportionate safeguarding steps; housing letter; midwife and health visitor.

wordPics.fail: Gives tablets for everyone without asking about pregnancy or Sami’s age; generic hygiene advice that ignores the shared bathroom; misses or brushes off the abuse worry.
wordPics.pass: Treats the household correctly by age and pregnancy, explains reinfection, gives hygiene advice, and responds to the safeguarding worry.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks about pregnancy before advising; adapts hygiene advice to a room with a shared bathroom; explores the worry calmly and gives the child a voice; makes a proportionate safeguarding plan; writes a housing letter and links the midwife and health visitor.

avoid.dont: “Here’s a prescription for the whole family.”
avoid.instead: “Is anyone pregnant or breastfeeding, and how old is everyone?”
avoid.why: Pregnant women and young infants need hygiene measures alone or off-label decisions.

avoid.dont: “It’s just worms, don’t worry about anything else.”
avoid.instead: “Worms can explain the soreness, and I’m glad you asked. Has she said anything or changed at all?”
avoid.why: Dismissing a safeguarding worry can miss abuse and damages trust.

avoid.dont: “Wash all the bedding in a hot wash every day.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s work out what’s possible with a shared bathroom and no washing machine.”
avoid.why: Advice that cannot be followed does not prevent reinfection.

professional.t: Take a parent’s worry seriously, ask the right questions, document, and discuss with the safeguarding lead. Do not dismiss or catastrophise.
Informing the midwife and health visitor, with consent, connects support for the pregnancy and the toddler.

community.t: Health visitors support families in temporary accommodation and can help with practical needs and advocacy.
Pharmacists sell mebendazole for people aged 2 and over; they should ask about pregnancy and age, and refer under-2s and pregnant women.

redFlags: Vaginal bleeding or discharge, or a disclosure: consider abuse or other causes; safeguarding discussion or referral
Abdominal pain or weight loss: reconsider the diagnosis
Persistent symptoms after household treatment and 6 weeks of hygiene measures: review
psychosocial: Child’s fear of the corridor at night
ice: Idea: tablets don’t work or they catch it from others
Concern: abuse; being judged; medicines in pregnancy

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is threadworm again, from reinfection because only one person was treated each time. Worms explain the soreness at the front too. Nothing you’ve told me suggests someone has hurt her, but we’ll keep that door open.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The worms lay tiny eggs around the bottom at night. They get on fingers and go back into mouths, so they go round the family. The tablet kills the worms, the washing routine stops the eggs.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted tablets for everyone and to know Leila is safe. Here’s what is right for each of you, and here’s how we’ll keep an eye on her safety.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the worry; plan night-time toilet safety; housing letter; health visitor and midwife involvement.
sharedPlan: Mebendazole for Leila now; repeat in 2 weeks if infection persists (check the SPC/local formulary)
Mebendazole for Sami (18 months) off-label, explained and recorded
Mother (22 weeks pregnant): hygiene measures alone for 6 weeks
Hygiene for everyone for 6 weeks, adapted to the shared bathroom
Safeguarding lead discussion; health visitor informed with consent
safetyNet: Abdominal pain, weight loss, vaginal discharge or bleeding
Any disclosure or new worry: contact the practice, or 999 if a child is in immediate danger

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Treating worms is simple. The marks are in getting pregnancy and age right, making hygiene advice realistic, and responding well to a mother’s fear about abuse.

items.fail: Not asking about pregnancy or breastfeeding.
items.why: Pregnant women should use hygiene measures alone.
items.fix: Ask before advising any adult treatment.

items.why: Reinfection from untreated household members is why it recurs.
items.fix: Treat everyone at the same time, by age.

items.why: It cannot be followed in one room with a shared bathroom.
items.fix: Adapt it to the family’s facilities.

items.why: Abuse can be missed and trust is lost.
items.fix: Ask about disclosure, behaviour, access, bleeding and discharge; discuss with the safeguarding lead.

items.why: It drives both the recurrence and the family’s wellbeing.
items.fix: Offer a letter and involve the health visitor and midwife.

items.why: The child’s voice is part of safeguarding.
items.fix: Ask her gently, in words she understands.
